```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = TRUE,
                      comment = "")

library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)

source("slides_setup.R", local = knitr::knit_global())

options(width = 70, pillar.print_min = 3, pillar.print_max = 3,
        readr.show_col_types = TRUE)

set.seed(42)
rt_data <- tibble(
  participant = rep(sprintf("P%02d", 1:10), each = 20),
  word        = rep(sprintf("w%02d", 1:20), times = 10),
  frequency   = rep(rep(c("high", "low"), each = 10), times = 10),
  rt          = round(rnorm(200, mean = 600, sd = 80) +
                        rep(rep(c(0, 60), each = 10), times = 10)),
  accuracy    = rbinom(200, size = 1, prob = 0.9)
)
```

## Today

<style>
  :root {
    --footer-text:  "Data wrangling";
    --qr:           `r qr_css`;

  }
</style>

By the end of this class you will be able to

- explain what the `tidyverse` is and what [tidy data]{.hl} looks like
- read and write `.csv` files with `{readr}`
- use the core `{dplyr}` verbs: `select()`, `filter()`, `arrange()`, `rename()`, `mutate()`
- summarise data by group with `summarise()` and `count()`
- chain everything together with the pipe `|>`

# The tidyverse

_"R is not a language driven by the purity of its philosophy; R is a language designed to get shit done."_

[Hadley Wickham]{.hl} (Chief Scientist at Posit, formerly RStudio)

## Tidyverse {.smaller}

A collection of R packages that share the same [design]{.hl}, [grammar]{.hl} and [data structures]{.hl}.

- A [dialect]{.hl} of R: everything you know from base R still works
- Functions are [verbs]{.hl} named after what they do
- The [data]{.hl} always comes first, so functions can be chained
- Output is (almost) always a [data frame]{.hl}, so the next step knows what to expect
- Together with [Quarto]{.hl} / [R Markdown]{.hl}: reproducible analyses

## Base R vs tidyverse {.smaller}

Same question: _mean body mass of Gentoo penguins, in kg_

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
[Base R]{.hl}

```{r, eval=FALSE}
gentoo <- penguins[penguins$species == "Gentoo", ]
mean(gentoo$body_mass_g / 1000, na.rm = TRUE)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
`tidyverse`

```{r, eval=FALSE}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Gentoo") |>
  summarise(mass_kg = mean(body_mass_g / 1000, na.rm = TRUE))
```
:::

::::

. . .

Neither is "wrong". The tidyverse version reads like a sentence.

## The core tidyverse {.smaller}

`library(tidyverse)` loads nine packages:

| Package | What it does |
|---|---|
| `readr` | read and write rectangular data (.csv, .tsv) |
| `tibble` | a modern data frame |
| `dplyr` | manipulate data: filter, select, mutate, summarise |
| `tidyr` | reshape data (wide to long and back) |
| `ggplot2` | plots |
| `stringr` | work with text |
| `forcats` | work with factors (categorical variables) |
| `lubridate` | work with dates and times |
| `purrr` | apply functions repeatedly (iteration) |

## The typical workflow {.smaller}

::: {style="text-align:center; font-size:1.1em;"}
[import]{.hl} → [tidy]{.hl} → [transform]{.hl} → [visualise]{.hl} → [model]{.hl} → [communicate]{.hl}
:::

- [import]{.hl}: `{readr}`
- [tidy]{.hl}: `{tidyr}`
- [transform]{.hl}: `{dplyr}` (today)
- [visualise]{.hl}: `{ggplot2}` (next class)
- [model]{.hl}: the rest of this course
- [communicate]{.hl}: [Quarto]{.hl}

## Tidy data {.smaller}

A data set is [tidy]{.hl} when

1. each [variable]{.hl} is a column
2. each [observation]{.hl} is a row
3. each [value]{.hl} is a cell

. . .

`Frequency` is a variable. Where is it?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}
[Untidy]{.hl} (wide)

| participant | rt_high | rt_low |
|---|---|---|
| P01 | 580 | 642 |
| P02 | 611 | 690 |
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
[Tidy]{.hl} (long)

| participant | frequency | rt |
|---|---|---|
| P01 | high | 580 |
| P01 | low | 642 |
| P02 | high | 611 |
| P02 | low | 690 |
:::

::::

## Tibbles

A `tibble` is a data frame with nicer defaults.

```{r}
penguins
```

- Prints only the first rows and the columns that fit
- Shows the [type]{.hl} of each column: `<fct>`, `<dbl>`, `<int>`, `<chr>`

## `glimpse()`

A transposed overview: one line per column.

```{r}
glimpse(penguins)
```

# Example data

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` the 344 rows of the `penguins` data are real birds: adult Adélie, Chinstrap and Gentoo penguins nesting near [Palmer Station]{.hl}, Antarctica, measured by Dr Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station LTER team from 2007 to 2009.

_Sources: Gorman, Williams & Fraser (2014), PLoS ONE; palmerpenguins documentation_
:::

## The `penguins` data

344 penguins, 3 species, 3 islands in the Palmer Archipelago (Antarctica).

```{r, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("palmerpenguins")
library(palmerpenguins)
```

## `penguins` in base R {.smaller}

`Heads up!` Since R 4.5.0, base R also ships a `penguins` data set, but with [shorter column names]{.hl}:

| `{palmerpenguins}` | base R ≥ 4.5.0 |
|---|---|
| `bill_length_mm` | `bill_len` |
| `bill_depth_mm` | `bill_dep` |
| `flipper_length_mm` | `flipper_len` |
| `body_mass_g` | `body_mass` |

. . .

In this course we always load `{palmerpenguins}` first. If you get `object 'bill_length_mm' not found`, you forgot!

# `{readr}`

## Reading and writing files {.smaller}

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
We use `{readr}` primarily to
:::

- `read_csv()`: read comma separated files
- `read_tsv()`: read tab separated files
- `read_csv2()`: semicolon separated, with decimal commas (German Excel exports)
- `read_delim()`: any other separator
- `write_csv()`: save a data frame as .csv

. . .

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(readr)
data <- read_csv("data/my_file.csv")

# ... do things with data ...

write_csv(data, "data/my_file_clean.csv")
```

## What `read_csv()` tells you {.smaller}

```{r, include=FALSE}
example_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write_csv(head(rt_data, 6), example_file)
```

```{r}
rt <- read_csv(example_file)
```

. . .

- [Rows]{.hl} and [columns]{.hl} read
- The [type]{.hl} it guessed for each column
- If a guess is wrong, set it yourself:

. . .

```{r, eval=FALSE}
rt <- read_csv("data/rt.csv",
               col_types = cols(participant = col_factor()))
```

## `read_csv()` vs `read.csv()`

| | `read_csv()` | `read.csv()` |
|---|---|---|
| Package | `{readr}` | base R |
| Returns | tibble | data.frame |
| Speed | fast | slower on large files |
| Reports column types | yes | no |

. . .

Use `read_csv()` (with an `_`) in this course.

# `{dplyr}`

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` Adélie penguins take their name from [Adélie Land]{.hl} in Antarctica, which the French explorer Jules Dumont d'Urville named after his wife, Adèle, in 1840.

_Source: Australian Antarctic Division_
:::

## The grammar of `{dplyr}`

Every `{dplyr}` verb works the same way:

1. The first argument is a [data frame]{.hl}
2. The other arguments say [what to do]{.hl}, using column names [without quotes]{.hl}
3. The output is a [new data frame]{.hl}

## Six verbs

| Verb | Works on | Does |
|---|---|---|
| `select()` | columns | keep or drop columns |
| `rename()` | columns | change column names |
| `mutate()` | columns | create or change columns |
| `filter()` | rows | keep rows that match a condition |
| `arrange()` | rows | sort rows |
| `summarise()` | groups | collapse many rows into one |

## The verb never changes your data {.smaller}

```{r}
filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo")
nrow(penguins)
```

. . .

Nothing happened to `penguins`! To keep the result, [assign]{.hl} it:

```{r}
gentoo <- filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo")
nrow(gentoo)
```

# Columns

## `select()`

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Choose columns to keep / drop
:::

```{r}
select(penguins, species, bill_length_mm)
```

. . .

Drop a column with `-`

```{r, eval=FALSE}
select(penguins, -year)
```

## `select()` helpers {.smaller}

Select by [name pattern]{.hl} or [type]{.hl} instead of typing every name:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
select(penguins, species:bill_depth_mm)   # a range of columns
select(penguins, starts_with("bill"))     # names starting with "bill"
select(penguins, ends_with("_mm"))        # names ending with "_mm"
select(penguins, contains("length"))      # names containing "length"
select(penguins, where(is.numeric))       # all numeric columns
select(penguins, sex, everything())       # move sex to the front
```

. . .

```{r}
select(penguins, ends_with("_mm"))
```

## `select()` by position

Also possible, but [fragile]{.hl}:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
select(penguins, 1, 3, 5)
select(penguins, 1:4)
select(penguins, -(1:5))
```

. . .

If the column order changes (new data export, a colleague's file), your code silently selects the [wrong]{.hl} columns. Prefer [names]{.hl}.

## `rename()` {.smaller}

`new_name = old_name`

```{r}
rename(penguins, Type = species)
```

. . .

`select()` can rename too, but drops everything you do not name:

```{r}
select(penguins, Type = species, bill_length_mm)
```

## `mutate()` {.smaller}

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Create [new]{.hl} columns, or [overwrite]{.hl} existing ones
:::

```{r}
penguins_2 <- mutate(penguins,
                     body_mass_kg = body_mass_g / 1000,
                     bill_ratio   = bill_length_mm / bill_depth_mm)
select(penguins_2, species, body_mass_kg, bill_ratio)
```

. . .

New columns are added at the [end]{.hl}. You can use a column you just created in the same `mutate()`.

## `mutate()` with conditions {.smaller}

`if_else()` for two outcomes

```{r, eval=FALSE}
mutate(penguins, size = if_else(body_mass_g > 4500, "large", "small"))
```

. . .

`case_when()` for more than two

```{r}
penguins_2 <- mutate(penguins,
  size = case_when(
    body_mass_g < 3500 ~ "small",
    body_mass_g < 4500 ~ "medium",
    body_mass_g >= 4500 ~ "large"
  )
)
count(penguins_2, size)
```

. . .

Conditions are checked [in order]{.hl}. Rows matching none of them get `NA`.

## `mutate()` on many columns: `across()` {.smaller}

`mutate_if()` and `mutate_all()` are [superseded]{.hl}: they still work, but are no longer developed. Use `across()`:

. . .

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# old
mutate_if(penguins, is.factor, as.character)

# new
mutate(penguins, across(where(is.factor), as.character))
```

. . .

`across(columns, function)`: _apply this function to these columns_

```{r, eval=FALSE}
mutate(penguins, across(ends_with("_mm"), \(x) x / 10))  # mm to cm
```

`\(x) x / 10` is a short way to write a small function: _take x, divide it by 10_.

# Rows

## `filter()`

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
Keep the rows where a [condition]{.hl} is `TRUE`
:::

```{r}
filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo")
```

## Comparison operators {.smaller}

| Operator | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `==` | equal to | `species == "Gentoo"` |
| `!=` | not equal to | `species != "Gentoo"` |
| `>`, `>=` | greater than (or equal) | `body_mass_g > 4000` |
| `<`, `<=` | less than (or equal) | `year <= 2008` |
| `%in%` | one of | `island %in% c("Biscoe", "Dream")` |
| `is.na()` | missing | `is.na(sex)` |

. . .

`=` assigns, `==` compares. `filter(penguins, species = "Gentoo")` gives an error.

## Combining conditions {.smaller}

`,` or `&`: both must be true (AND)

```{r, eval=FALSE}
filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo", body_mass_g > 5000)
filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo" & body_mass_g > 5000)
```

. . .

`|`: at least one must be true (OR)

```{r, eval=FALSE}
filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo" | species == "Chinstrap")
```

. . .

`%in%` is shorter when matching several values of one column

```{r}
unique(filter(penguins, species %in% c("Gentoo", "Chinstrap"))$species)
```

## `filter()` and missing values {.smaller}

`filter()` drops rows where the condition is `NA`.

```{r}
nrow(penguins)
sum(is.na(penguins$sex))
nrow(filter(penguins, sex == "female"))
nrow(filter(penguins, sex != "female"))
```

. . .

`165 + 168 = 333`, not [344]{.hl}! The 11 penguins with unknown `sex` are dropped by [both]{.hl}.

## `filter_out()` (new in `{dplyr}` 1.2.0) {.smaller}

Say which rows to [drop]{.hl}. Rows with `NA` are [kept]{.hl}.

```{r}
nrow(filter_out(penguins, sex == "female"))
```

. . .

Rule of thumb:

- `filter()` when you know what to [keep]{.hl}
- `filter_out()` when you know what to [drop]{.hl}

. . .

Requires `{dplyr}` ≥ 1.2.0. Check with `packageVersion("dplyr")`.

## `arrange()`

Sort rows, smallest first

```{r}
arrange(penguins, body_mass_g)
```

. . .

Largest first with `desc()`; sort by several columns in turn

```{r, eval=FALSE}
arrange(penguins, desc(body_mass_g))
arrange(penguins, species, desc(body_mass_g))
```

# Groups

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` chinstrap penguins sleep in [microsleeps]{.hl}: more than 10,000 a day, about 4 seconds each, which add up to about 11 hours of sleep.

_Source: Libourel et al. (2023), Science_
:::

## `summarise()` {.smaller}

Collapse many rows into [one]{.hl}

```{r}
summarise(penguins,
          mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
          sd_mass   = sd(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
          n         = n())
```

. . .

`na.rm = TRUE`: ignore missing values. Without it, one `NA` makes the whole result `NA`.

## `group_by()` + `summarise()` {.smaller}

One row [per group]{.hl}

```{r}
penguins_grouped <- group_by(penguins, species)
summarise(penguins_grouped,
          mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
          n         = n())
```

. . .

`group_by()` changes nothing you can see. It tells the [next]{.hl} verb to work group by group.

## `.by`: grouping for one step {.smaller}

Same result, without a separate `group_by()`:

```{r}
summarise(penguins,
          mean_mass = mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE),
          n         = n(),
          .by       = c(species, sex))
```

. . .

`.by` groups for this verb only, so you never forget to `ungroup()`. It works in `summarise()`, `mutate()`, `filter()` and `slice()`.

## `count()`

A shortcut for counting rows per group

```{r}
count(penguins, species, island)
```

. . .

Same counts as `summarise(penguins, n = n(), .by = c(species, island))`, but `count()` also sorts the rows by group.

# The pipe

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` gentoo penguins are the [fastest swimming birds]{.hl}: they reach about 36 km/h in short bursts, close to Usain Bolt's average speed in his 100 m world record.

_Source: Guinness World Records_
:::

## The problem {.smaller}

Three steps, three intermediate objects:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
penguins_2 <- filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo" | species == "Chinstrap")
penguins_3 <- mutate(penguins_2, bill_length_cm = bill_length_mm / 10)
penguins_4 <- select(penguins_3, species, bill_length_cm)
```

. . .

Or nested, read from the [inside out]{.hl}:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
penguins_4 <- select(
  mutate(
    filter(penguins, species == "Gentoo" | species == "Chinstrap"),
    bill_length_cm = bill_length_mm / 10),
  species, bill_length_cm)
```

## The pipe `|>` {.smaller}

::: {.fragment .fade-up}
`x |> f(y)` is the same as `f(x, y)`
:::

- Takes the result on the [left]{.hl}, passes it as the [first argument]{.hl} of the function on the [right]{.hl}
- Read it aloud as [then]{.hl}
- No need to [repeat the object]{.hl} at every step

. . .

```{r}
penguins_2 <- penguins |>
  filter(species == "Gentoo" | species == "Chinstrap") |>
  mutate(bill_length_cm = bill_length_mm / 10) |>
  select(species, bill_length_cm)
penguins_2
```

## Reading a pipe aloud

```{r, eval=FALSE}
penguins_2 <- penguins |>
  filter(species == "Gentoo" | species == "Chinstrap") |>
  mutate(bill_length_cm = bill_length_mm / 10) |>
  select(species, bill_length_cm)
```

Take `penguins`, [then]{.hl} `filter` only the `species` Gentoo [or]{.hl} Chinstrap, [then]{.hl} `mutate` to add a column `bill_length_cm` which divides `bill_length_mm` by [10]{.hl}, [then]{.hl} `select` only `species` and `bill_length_cm`. Save the result as `penguins_2`.

## `PRO TIP!` Save to the right

```{r, eval=FALSE}
penguins |>
  filter(species == "Gentoo" | species == "Chinstrap") |>
  mutate(bill_length_cm = bill_length_mm / 10) |>
  select(species, bill_length_cm) -> penguins_2
```

Same output as the previous slide. The code now reads top to bottom in the order things happen.

## `|>` vs `%>%` {.smaller}

You will see two pipes in the wild:

- `%>%` from `{magrittr}`, loaded with the tidyverse (since 2014)
- `|>` built into R itself (since R 4.1.0)

. . .

For everything in this course they are [interchangeable]{.hl}. We use `|>`: it works without loading any package.

. . .

Keyboard shortcut: `Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + M`

To make it insert `|>`: _Tools > Global Options > Code > Use native pipe operator_

## From wrangling to plotting

The output of a pipe can go straight into `{ggplot2}`

```{r penguin-plot, eval=FALSE}
penguins |>
  filter_out(is.na(sex)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Flipper length (mm)", y = "Body mass (g)", colour = NULL)
```

. . .

Note: `{ggplot2}` layers are added with `+`, not `|>`. More next class.

## From wrangling to plotting

```{r, ref.label="penguin-plot", echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.5, out.width="100%"}
```

# Common errors

## Common errors {.smaller}

| You wrote | Problem |
|---|---|
| `filter(df, species = "Gentoo")` | `=` instead of `==` |
| `filter(df, species == Gentoo)` | text values need `"quotes"` |
| `select(df, Species)` | names are [case sensitive]{.hl} |
| `filter(df, ...)` and nothing changes | result not [assigned]{.hl} with `<-` |
| `mean(body_mass_g)` gives `NA` | missing values: add `na.rm = TRUE` |
| `object 'bill_length_mm' not found` | forgot `library(palmerpenguins)` |
| `could not find function "filter_out"` | `{dplyr}` older than 1.2.0 |

## Summary

::: {.takeaway}
- `{readr}`: `read_csv()`, `write_csv()`
- Columns: `select()`, `rename()`, `mutate()`, `across()`
- Rows: `filter()`, `filter_out()`, `arrange()`
- Groups: `summarise()`, `count()`, `group_by()` or `.by`
- Chain with `|>`, read as [then]{.hl}
- Always [assign]{.hl} the result if you want to keep it
:::
